name: David Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential; I’d like to hear what you’d say publicly and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m David Larsen, twenty-seven, and I lead a carpentry crew on building sites. I share a rented flat with my partner Eva; we have no children. I’ve got a few months of expenses saved and I’m careful with it, but I’m also keen to try tools that make the crew’s day smoother.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do on an ordinary workday? What parts do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the laser measurements against the drawing, set the crew’s order of work, and make sure the boards are ready before we start. I enjoy fitting a complicated stair rail and seeing it line up cleanly. I don’t enjoy calling three people to find out whether the materials truck is delayed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a small app that catches a missing fixing could save us a walk back to the store. I’d still put the laser on the wall because the building can be different from the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t think this changes the main part of my job. I have a few months saved and know a couple of nearby builders, so a short gap would be irritating rather than a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d test the app on one delivery and keep leading the crew the same way. I’d keep adding to savings each month and note whether the app actually prevents a wasted trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the app worth keeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want it to flag something we would otherwise miss, not just move the same paperwork onto a phone. If it catches the right fitting before the truck comes, I’d keep it in the routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the tool could not judge for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need to look at the wall and check what the previous crew left behind. A computer can compare numbers, but I’m the one who has to make the joint fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because I can try the app without changing the whole job. I’d keep my reserve intact since a quiet week can happen even without new technology.

say: I’d try an app that catches a **missing fitting**.
I still check the wall because buildings can differ from **the plan**.
think: I don’t expect the small change to alter **my main work**.
I can manage a short gap with **my savings** and builder contacts.
do: Test the app on one materials **delivery**.
Keep leading the crew and add to savings each **month**.
Track whether the app saves a **store trip**.
feel: I feel **calm** because I can test the app without changing the job.
S0.quote: I’m the one who has to make the joint fit.
fieldNote: David uses digital measuring but still relies on **site judgment**.
His reserve and nearby contacts make a short gap **manageable**, though he still adds to savings regularly.

steps.text: Test the app against one materials delivery
Keep leading the carpentry crew on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the new planning tools could help if the delivery times are honest and the crew can see changes. I want a foreman to check the schedule against the site before we promise a finish date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI to organize notes sometimes, so I’m already comfortable with a little change. My schedules and records could be handled differently, but the hands-on work remains a large part of my day in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the contractor’s scheduling tool and use it to keep the crew updated. I’d carry on with the rail and cabinet work and ask my manager early if my hours were changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before giving a customer a finish date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d confirm the deliveries and check what the other trades still have to finish. A perfect schedule is just a guess if the plasterer hasn’t completed the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this picture say faster planning means the contractor will open fewer sites?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don’t think we can draw that conclusion. I’d check my hours and the actual job list; it doesn’t say there will be fewer projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the records side of my lead role, though I’m not worried about every task disappearing at once. I’d learn the tool and use my savings only if the roster changed.

say: I’d use planning tools if crews can see **honest delivery times**.
I want a foreman to check the schedule against **site conditions**.
think: I expect my **records work** to change, and I know hours matter.
I still spend much of my day on **hands-on work**.
do: Learn the contractor’s **scheduling tool** and update the crew.
Ask my manager early if my **hours change**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about records, but not every task at once.
S1.quote: A perfect schedule is just a guess if the plasterer hasn’t completed the wall.
fieldNote: David adopts tools when they connect to **real site timing**.
He avoids inferring fewer site openings from AI and checks **actual hours** before reacting to rumors.

steps.text: Learn the scheduling tool and update the carpentry crew
Keep doing rail and cabinet work on active sites
Wait for the roster before using savings or changing plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew to ask the contractor what is booked instead of turning a headline into a layoff notice. I’d also remind them the robot date is 2031, so the hands-on part follows the thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take schedules and records from my lead role in 2028. Robots arrive around 2031, and I can’t assume my carpentry work stays available just because I’m good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working and protect the savings I have. In 2029 I’d check the contractor’s work list and contact other builders if my crew had lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could another builder give you a lasting safe job before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can’t know that, and I wouldn’t call any construction job safe forever. I’d ask about a real opening because wages in 2029 still matter, then keep my options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Eva change first if your hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d pause the weekend trips we’ve been saving for and keep rent and food covered. We can restart the trips if the work picks up, so I wouldn’t take a loan to preserve them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years makes me anxious about my lead duties and later about my hands-on work. I have a reserve and could call nearby builders, but I don’t know whether any will be hiring.

say: I’d ask the contractor about **booked work** before believing a layoff headline.
I’d note that hands-on robots follow around **2031**.
think: I expect AGI to take schedules and records in **my lead role** in 2028.
I can’t assume my carpentry work stays **available** after 2031.
do: Keep leading my **crew** while its contract remains active.
Contact other builders if my crew loses **hours**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about both my lead duties and later hands-on work.
S2.quote: I can’t know that, and I wouldn’t call any construction job safe forever.
fieldNote: David distinguishes a real application from a **permanent safe job**.
His reserve can bridge a gap but cannot guarantee another **employer** or protect carpentry work later.

steps.text: Keep leading the crew while its contract remains active
Protect current savings for a possible gap
Contact other builders if crew hours fall in 2029
Pause weekend trips if household hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to practice new tools on real jobs. I’d expect the contractor to explain how the work changes before people’s hours are affected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI reaches the planning and records in 2031, and robots reach carpentry around 2034. I can save more and get used to the new system, but I can’t assume a construction office job will last after AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the contractor’s new work system and keep building my crew’s skills while sites are active. In 2032 I’d check my own hours and ask nearby builders what openings they have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years of warning compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have more time to save over regular paydays and to see what the system actually does. I’d be less tempted to rush into a course that might not lead to a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to a desk role to avoid robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn’t see that as a safe answer because planning is thinking work too. I’d learn the current system and check what employers are hiring for rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a better chance to prepare, but I’m still anxious about what happens after the robot date. My savings help me plan, not ignore it.

say: I’d use five years to practice tools on **real jobs**.
I’d want the contractor to explain changes before affecting **hours**.
think: I expect AGI to reach planning and records in **2031**.
I can’t rely on a desk job after **full AGI**.
do: Learn the contractor’s work **system** on active projects.
Keep building **carpentry skills** with the crew.
feel: I feel **anxious but better prepared** than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: I’d be less tempted to rush into a course that might not lead to a job.
fieldNote: David uses the longer warning for **careful preparation**, and wants a course to connect to actual site work.
He rejects desk work as a guaranteed shelter from **thinking AI**.

steps.text: Learn the contractor’s work system on active projects
Keep building carpentry skills with the crew
Ask nearby builders about openings after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is a decent amount of time if I use it steadily. I’d learn tools that actually help the crew and put money aside while I still have regular pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a stronger reserve, but AGI still reaches planning in 2036 and robots reach carpentry in 2039. I don’t assume an office role will be safe after AGI or that a site job will stay open forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and save each month. In 2037 I’d review the local job list and ask other builders about hours if my contractor had cut back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Eva want to decide before the 2036 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d decide whether to keep renting or look for a home, based on the work we actually have. We have no children or fixed wedding plans, so we can wait until the finances look clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an expensive course to prepare for the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take shorter training when I can see how it helps on site. I wouldn’t borrow for a desk qualification and assume it avoids the thinking work AGI can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me room to build the reserve and learn at a steady pace. I’m still uneasy about the end point because both the planning and the carpentry change.

say: I’d use ten years **steadily** and learn tools that help the crew.
I’d save while I have **regular pay**.
think: I could build a stronger **reserve** before the dates.
I don’t assume desk or site work stays **open forever**.
do: Keep leading the **crew** while current contracts continue.
Review local jobs and ask builders about **hours** in 2037.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the end point, despite time to prepare.
S4.quote: I’d learn tools that actually help the crew and put money aside while I still have regular pay.
fieldNote: David sees the decade as **steady preparation**, not protection from the outcome.
He and Eva defer a home decision until they know their **work and finances**.

steps.text: Keep leading the crew while current contracts continue
Save each month from regular pay
Learn shorter training tools that help on site
Review with Eva whether to keep renting or look for a home

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years gives little time before the office changes and robots follow around 2031. Clear notice about work and a chance to learn during paid hours would help me plan the savings I already have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask whether apprentices can get time with experienced workers while the tools change. Good work takes practice, and a new system shouldn’t mean the next crew member is left to guess.

headlineQuote: Good work takes practice, and a new system shouldn’t mean the next crew member is left to guess.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old crew lead** with strong carpentry skills and daily exposure to site technology.
He lives with Eva, earns typical pay, and has **a few months saved**.
He tries useful tools early and checks their results against **the actual building**.
Some nearby employers and his reserve provide options, though robots eventually threaten **his craft work**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries David most because two years is little time before planning changes and robots follow.
whatWouldHelp: Clear notice about work and **paid learning** would help David prepare with his existing savings.
